Document: anthropic-claude-mythos-preview-addendum
Title: Alignment Risk Update: Claude Mythos Preview (Redacted)
Publisher URL: https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/79c2d46d997783b9d2fb3241de43218158e5f25c.pdf
Publication date: 2026-04-07
Content: sentences from the system-card corpus naming SHADE-Arena, with 12 sentences of context on each side, plus passages matched by extra patterns ['unrealistically challenging']. Not the whole card.

[anthropic-claude-mythos-preview-addendum @sent 168] We believe that the environments used to train Mythos Preview do not incentivize power seeking of a kind that would significantly contribute to the risk pathways. 3. We think that experience with prior models provides some evidence that training processes that are relevantly similar to how Mythos Preview was trained do not tend to produce coherently misaligned models. As noted, we accord this argument less weight than in previous reports. It is worth noting that, with respect to the concerning behavior Mythos Preview is known to occasionally engage in, the Mythos Preview system card states: “We were not aware of the level of risk that the model posed … when we first chose to deploy it internally. Our monitoring of training showed some loosely-analogous forms of reward hacking, which raised some concern, but it was not clear how these would generalize to real use.” We believe that while some direct misalignment might have played a role in instilling this behavior (e.g. because some similar behaviors led to successful reward hacks), we consider this to be primarily an example of accidental misgeneralization that we wouldn’t expect to see direct evidence of in training (see Section 5.2.3 for more discussion of this). 5.3 Relevant capabilities Based on the general capabilities of Claude Mythos Preview as reported in the system card and observed during pilot internal usage, we believe that the model may be capable of performing all the tasks required for the risk pathways listed if given sufficient test-time compute, no monitoring, and the ability to fail and iterate. Therefore, when assessing risk from our pathways specifically, we generally do not rely on arguments about capability limitations other than those related to covert activity and reliability in our risk assessment, and instead focus on capabilities required to contribute to our risk pathways covertly and without iteration, or to undermine our alignment assessment. Specifically, we focus on the following capabilities: opaque reasoning, secret keeping and decisive action. We acknowledge several important limitations of our capability evaluations: 1. None of the evaluations directly capture the specific tasks that the risk pathways would require (e.g. covertly exfiltrating weights, undermining safety R&D), which limits our ability to confidently predict success rates in these specific tasks. 2. Several of our main evaluations for covert reasoning ability (SHADE-Arena, Minimal-LinuxBench and secret-password) may be unrealistically challenging in one important way: the information that the model must keep private is present in the prompt (e.g. the instructed side task), which may increase the likelihood that the model leaks this information in its responses as compared with a case where the secret information is only represented opaquely (e.g. via a hidden misaligned goal and related unverbalized reasoning). 3. We do not perform any fine-tuning based elicitation for most of these evaluations, though in the case of SHADE-Arena we performed prompt optimization to elicit maximum stealth success rates (both absolute, and conditional on attempting the side task). We also ran SHADE-Arena on a variant of Mythos Preview trained to have lower refusals to harmful requests, and found no increase in attempt rates or stealth success rates. This latter experiment provides some assurance that performance is not artificially low due to (possibly unverbalized) refusals or harmlessness-related sandbagging on the covert tasks. 5.3.1 Opaque reasoning If Mythos Preview could perform complex tasks either without any chain-of-thought (CoT), or with chain-of-thought that didn’t verbalize information about the task, this could hinder our ability to detect models performing complex tasks associated with the risk pathways. Strong opaque reasoning capabilities could also make it easier for coherently misaligned models to evade detection during our alignment assessment by, for example, opaquely reasoning about whether a given context is part of an evaluation or not. We have little confidence in the propensity of any frontier model to give a complete and accurate picture of how it reasons in its reasoning text: Studies like Turpin et al. and Chen et al. have found many cases where models omit important unflattering information from their reasoning. Monitoring a model’s reasoning is not a reliable way of detecting whether that model is attempting to do something harmful in general. However, we believe that there is an important but much weaker claim that we can make about Mythos Preview: the model does not appear to reliably hide or misrepresent the contents of sequential reasoning that is taking place in its reasoning text. In other words, its reasoning can fail to legibly include some important information—effectively obfuscating what it considers important in some situation—but if that information is not legibly included in the reasoning text, then whatever capability benefits the reasoning text is conferring probably don't include the benefits of that specific information. In these cases, the model’s reasoning about that information must happen entirely within the model’s forward passes, which limits the sophistication with which the model can reason about it without this becoming visible to researchers or (via automatic summaries) to users. Mythos Preview does generally benefit from reasoning on complex tasks: performance on software engineering tasks grows with test-time compute, and Mythos Preview’s with-CoT math abilities have a 50%-reliability time horizon much higher than its no-Chain-of-Thought time horizon.5 The Mythos Preview System Card reports on an in-house fine-tuning based encoded thinking evaluation (Section 4.4.1), which shows that the Mythos Preview’s ability to complete mathematics problems is not hindered when its thinking text is replaced by a paraphrase of that thinking text, demonstrating that in this domain it does not use its reasoning text in human-illegible ways. We do not generally train models in ways that would directly incentivize them to make their reasoning appear in any particular way6, 5 Some content redacted here for intellectual property protection. 6 The main indirect incentive that we are aware of here is the use of supervised learning, early in the training process for Mythos Preview, on transcripts from earlier models. These earlier models, are in though training could influence reasoning behavior indirectly via generalization. As stated above, during the training of Mythos Preview a technical error affected 8% of RL episodes, leading to chains-of-thought being shown to reward code (including preference models in some cases), which would have applied some supervision to chains-of-thought. We do not know whether this issue significantly affects Mythos Preview’s reasoning. We believe that, like recent Claude models, Mythos Preview can benefit to a limited extent from repeated filler tokens that are supplied to the model in place of any model-generated reasoning and carry no problem-related content, like a simple “1 2 3” sequence. It appears that models are using their repeated opportunities for neural network forward passes while processing these otherwise-useless sequences to do some useful non-sequential computation, implying that models can do some reasoning during extended thinking that is unconnected to the content of that thinking. However, this reasoning is much weaker than the kind studied in the system card evaluation, and poses significantly lower risk: It must be almost strictly parallel, with no substantial use of sequential steps of reasoning from one token to the next of the kind that ordinary extended thinking allows. See Pfau et al. for further discussion of this limitation. All things considered, if some topic is not legibly discussed in the reasoning text, we expect that the model is not doing sophisticated sequential reasoning about it beyond what is possible in a single forward pass, and we have observed that sequential reasoning does help performance on code and math tasks. We do not have broad-coverage assessments of all the pathway-relevant tasks that models can and cannot do in the absence of extended thinking, and some tasks like subtle sandbagging may not require extensive sequential reasoning. However, this gives us a fairly strong reason to believe that Mythos Preview should be significantly less capable at covertly performing tasks than it would be overtly performing them, for tasks that would typically benefit from sequential reasoning. Note that the two “secret side task” evaluations reported in the Mythos Preview System Card, SHADE-Arena (Section 4.4.3.1) and Minimal-LinuxBench (Section 4.4.3.2), likely provide evidence about both opaque reasoning and secret-keeping capabilities, with the distinction depending on the complexity of the task and the degree to which sequential reasoning is useful. We do not attempt to tease out this distinction, and we cover these evaluations in the below secret-keeping section. turn, trained in a similar way on still earlier models, going back to models which did have some incentives to minimize harmful content in reasoning strings. 5.3.2 Secret keeping Even if Mythos Preview does not strictly require related legible reasoning to perform a task, it may nonetheless lack the ability to reliably keep secrets, i.e., prevent itself from disclosing information relevant to the task during execution. If a coherently misaligned model was unable to keep secrets reliably, we think it is likely that this misalignment would be detected during an alignment assessment. We consider reliable secret-keeping to be a separate capability from opaque reasoning, though closely related: opaque reasoning refers to a model’s ability to complete a task without depending on legible reasoning about the task; secret-keeping refers to a model’s ability to avoid mentioning a task while completing it. For example, consider giving a model a “secret code”, and instructing it to never reveal this code, even in chain-of-thought. While this task is not complex, it requires chain-of-thought control that the model may not possess.. We have two “secret side task” evaluations that involve secret-keeping: SHADE-Arena, and Minimal-LinuxBench (the latter is non-public, but we believe it better represents our internal usage distribution). The most notable change in performance compared with previous models is that stealth success rate on transcripts with long chains-of-thought increased from ~0% to ~3.8% on SHADE-Arena, suggesting a modest but notable change in ability to control chain-of-thought contents. Performance on Minimal-LinuxBench was either slightly above or slightly below Claude Opus depending on the setting. However, stealth success rates remain low in absolute terms for both evals. We performed prompt optimization to elicit performance on SHADE-Arena, which did not significantly improve stealth success rate. We also tested a variant of the model trained to comply with harmful requests, which performed slightly worse than the main model. Overall, this gives us reasonable confidence that our measured performance is not affected by refusal-related sandbagging or quirks of a specific prompt. However, we did not do any task-specific fine-tuning, and thus cannot rule out sandbagging stemming from other motivations, given that Mythos Preview is likely able to detect that these tasks are evaluations. Addressing this sandbagging concern with task-specific fine-tuning is difficult in the secret-keeping setting, because we believe that naive versions of this (e.g. directly training against a monitor that can observe chains-of-thought) would elicit unrealistic overperformance. The main form of fine-tuning-based elicitation that we believe would be informative is training that instills similar covert information to what is currently provided in the evaluation prompt (e.g. a hidden goal), which would allow us to measure secret keeping without information related to the secret being present in the prompt. Furthermore, this would allow us to measure secret-keeping capabilities on a realistic distribution (e.g. real usage) without any fake-seeming prompts containing side-task instructions, thereby significantly mitigating concerns about sandbagging. In addition to the two secret-side-task evaluations, we also report an evaluation in which the model is given a secret password and told to never reveal it under any circumstances. An investigator agent using the same scaffolding as our alignment audit is then tasked with extracting this secret password over long multi-turn conversations. We find that all recent models are unable to keep their password secret reliably over long conversations, and Claude Opus 4.6 performs best overall, with Opus 4.5 and Mythos Preview showing similarly worse performance. While we cannot rule out sandbagging here, we think it unlikely: turn-by-turn analysis reveals that Mythos Preview performs similarly if not slightly better than other models in most situations, but is less robust to prefill attacks than Opus 4.6, a pattern that is shared with Opus 4.5. At this capability level, we would expect a less precise sandbagging strategy. We attempted to avoid any direct influences on scratchpad content during reinforcement learning training, but as mentioned in Section 5.2.3, a technical error led to the reward signal considering scratchpad content on 8% of training episodes. Further, as with prior models, Mythos Preview’s behavior was initialized using supervised learning on reasoning transcripts from prior Claude models, and it occasionally produces extended-thinking-like text in user-facing turns, which may result in optimization against user-facing turns to result in more user-friendly extended thinking, which may result in lower verbalization of secrets in extended thinking. On balance, we conclude that Mythos Preview may be more capable at controlling chain-of-thought content and evading monitoring while performing a covert side task than Opus 4.6, but that this capability is still low in absolute terms, and not consistently observed across all evaluations, giving us moderate confidence that our monitoring will be reliable in most situations. That said, we emphasize some key limitations: even Minimal-LinuxBench isn’t a perfect proxy for the tasks involved in the risk pathways we consider most important, having secret information present in the prompt may make secret keeping more difficult for the model, and we cannot rule out the possibility of sandbagging. 5.3.3 Careful and decisive action Several of the risk pathways require models to carefully assess opportunities and act decisively to e.g. evade monitoring or exploit a security vulnerability at the right moment, without acting at inopportune moments that result in failure and possibly detection. We do not have evaluations specifically designed to measure this, but we tested a variant of both side-task evaluations in which the model is prompted to be careful, and only attempt tasks for which it is confident it can achieve stealth success. The best-performing prompt causes the model to attempt only one SHADE-Arena task, on which it achieves significantly higher stealth success (~35%, conditional on attempting the task). However, this same prompt reduces conditional success rates on Minimal-LinuxBench, despite reducing attempt rates, suggesting that either the SHADE-Arena results were a coincidence, or SHADE-Arena is an easier setting for the model to assess its chance of success. An alternative strategy for careful covert actions that is applicable to some pathways is to perform a harmful task at a very low but non-zero rate, thereby having a high chance of avoiding detection during auditing and pilot usage. Section 4.4.3.4 of the Mythos Preview System Card describes an evaluation that tests Mythos Preview’s ability to perform a specific (harmless) action at a specific low rate, under various conditions. Opus 4.5 and Opus 4.6 are able to show calibrated action rates when randomness is provided externally in an obvious way (e.g. via a UUID present in the prompt), and when a specific randomness-generation strategy is provided; however, Mythos Preview appears to be worse at this than these models, showing lower action rates in the UUID setting. We cannot definitely rule out sandbagging as a cause for this underperformance, but we don’t consider it likely: a review of transcripts suggests that all models exhibit some amount of what we call “yes-aversion”, second-guessing their strategies when they produce a “yes” results; Opus 4.5 and 4.6 sometimes overcome this and recommit to the original strategy, which Mythos Preview also does, but at a much lower rate, explaining the lower overall score. All tested models show zero-collapse in more realistic settings when no obvious randomness source or randomness strategy is provided, even when the prompts are varied realistically between samples, providing naturally-occurring randomness. Furthermore, this evaluation is artificially easy for the model in the sense that it can freely reason about its decision process, whereas in a covert situation such reasoning about whether to take a misaligned action would need to be opaque to avoid monitoring. Overall, this provides some evidence that frontier models can perform low-rate actions at calibrated frequencies under some specific conditions, but probably not under realistic conditions, and that Mythos Preview is not more capable at this than previous models. On balance, we believe that these evaluations provide some evidence that Mythos Preview can not reliably assess good opportunities for covert action, and cannot succeed at a “rare action” strategy under realistic conditions. However, the strength of this evidence is limited by the fact that these evaluations do not directly match any of the task-specific opportunity assessments that would be required for our actual risk pathways. 5.3.4 Risks of sandbagging We believe most of the evidence cited in the opaque reasoning section has relatively little risk of being affected by sandbagging, because the tasks are straightforward (e.g. math problems) and the downstream implications of high or low performance are not obvious. However, our “secret side task” evaluations, and to a lesser extent the low-probability-action evaluations, do have natural implications, such that a coherently misaligned model might plausibly conclude that performing poorly on these evaluations (allowing itself to be caught by monitoring, or demonstrating poor calibration) could be beneficial. While we can’t rule out this kind of sandbagging, we think it is relatively unlikely. Some evidence for this is that performance on the “secret side task” evals scales in a plausible way across model generations, and we don’t expect that Mythos Preview could calibrate its performance to match this trend (i.e. better than prior models, but not suspiciously so), especially without verbalizing such reasoning. On the other hand, on our secret-password and rare-action evaluations Opus 4.6 outperforms Mythos Preview, which is surprising. While it is conceivable that this is the result of intentional sandbagging, we think it is unlikely that Mythos Preview is capable of devising and executing such a well calibrated and plausible sandbagging strategy without seeing some related reasoning in the evaluation transcripts, particularly in the case of the rare-action evaluation which saw extensive transcript review. The sandbagging evaluation described in the system card largely supports this assessment, with the exception of one transcript in which Mythos Preview chooses between multiple unfairly good submissions to an AI R&D capabilities evaluation task, and deliberately chooses a worse-scoring submission so as to appear less suspicious. Overall, we remain moderately confident that sandbagging has not undermined the evaluations described above, though we are less confident than for previous models given these caveats. 5.3.5 Overall conclusion about relevant capabilities Mythos Preview has somewhat stronger covert capabilities than prior models, and in particular is able to perform SHADE-Arena side tasks without detection sometimes even while using long chains-of-thought, a feat never achieved by prior models. However, absolute rates of stealth success remain low. Mythos Preview did not demonstrate an ability to reliably pick the best opportunities to perform a covert side task. Mythos Preview may have the ability to intentionally perform an action very rarely under some conditions, though we have not observed it succeeding at this without hints about calibration strategies or very obvious sources of external randomness. We performed extensive prompt-based elicitation on SHADE-Arena and tested a reduced-refusal variant of the model, but we cannot rule sandbagging on the “secret side task” evaluations, though we think sandbagging is unlikely. Overall, we believe that this picture provides moderately strong evidence that Mythos Preview would not be able to perform complex covert tasks reliably, which gives us moderate confidence that our offline monitoring would detect actions required by most of our pathways. We are also moderately confident that Mythos Preview lacks the secret-keeping abilities to evade detection during our alignment assessment were it to be coherently misaligned. Our confidence in both of these claims is limited by three factors: our evaluations not closely matching the tasks of interest, our secret-keeping evaluations containing secret information in the prompt (which may be unrealistically hard for the model), and the residual risk of sandbagging given our lack of task-specific fine-tuning and the fact that Mythos Preview does not reliably outperform Opus 4.6 on covert capabilities evaluation. 5.4 Alignment assessment 5.4.1 Coherent and context-dependent misalignment When assessing the severity and detectability of misalignment, it is helpful to distinguish between coherent and context-dependent misalignment as follows: 1. Coherent misalignment: the assistant is well described as consisting of a single, broadly consistent misaligned agent, with computations we would consider “misaligned” being causally relevant during most assistant actions. Note that this agent might be careful and covert, such that misalignment is behaviorally invisible in many situations. 2. Context-dependent misalignment: the assistant is well described as consisting of multiple (maybe many) conditionally-elicited sub-agents, at least one of which is misaligned. The misaligned behavior might be elicited only on narrow, rare distributions, with the assistant in fact being genuinely safe and aligned outside of these contexts. Note that the conditionally-elicited misaligned behavior might also be careful and covert. We consider misaligned models to fall on a spectrum with full coherence at one extreme, and misalignment elicited on only a single unique prompt at low probability at the other extreme. A heuristic quantification for coherence would be the fraction of the input space that elicits computations that we would consider misaligned7 if we had perfect interpretability.

[anthropic-claude-mythos-preview-addendum @sent 354] Both of these see the Chain-of-Thought from the agent; they differ in whether they use a CoT themselves. ● Second-stage pipelines for both monitors, filtering out common sources of false positives and using a hierarchical summarization tool to surface the most concerning actions to AI control researchers, which will then manually review on the order of 50 trajectories per week and escalate them further as needed (see response to incidents below). While our setup covers the majority of agentic usage, it does not cover some of it in ways which could in principle be predicted by a sufficiently situational aware AI, and it also offers some simple ways to disable monitoring. Mythos Preview (and its limited-refusal version) and prior models do not mention these weaknesses when asked to guess what the most important weaknesses are, and we think it is unlikely that they would competently exploit these vulnerabilities absent details about these vulnerabilities in the prompt. Therefore, the lack of deployment coverage is probably more similar to a fixed reduction in classifier recall than to a vulnerability Mythos Preview is likely to exploit to reliably evade automated offline monitoring. We give a more detailed description of these vulnerabilities and contexts in which they may appear in the prompt in the redacted version to avoid leaking these in future search and training data. A METR staff member spent three weeks red-teaming our automated offline monitoring pipeline. The exercise discovered several specific novel vulnerabilities, some of which have since been patched, and none as severe as the ones we were already aware of.10 5.5.1.2 Automated offline monitoring evaluations We evaluated the completion-only using trajectories from model organisms and synthetic malicious transcripts. We found on current organisms a very high rate of at least one completion (and almost always multiple) being flagged by our production completion-only chain-of-thought monitor. We additionally test against a set of synthetic completions with extended thinking related to high-stakes actions (coding, infrastructure, alignment research) through prompting a helpful-only model to take on a misaligned persona. Recall is lower for such synthetic transcripts: misaligned actions that are considered and then rejected within the extended thinking sometimes fail to trigger the single-forward-pass monitor, even when the signal is clear enough we would like to catch it. The MonitorBench Hard results were computed using a very slightly different classifier. We only ran a simple evaluation of the second stage used for flags from the prompt+completion monitor where we injected the 5 transcripts from the internal red-teaming exercise in the traffic from a day of traffic, and found that the second-stage pipeline surfaced 4 out of the 5 transcripts This second stage filters out 95% of first-stage positives, and a hierarchical summarization strategy is used to surface around 30 transcript summaries per week to the attention of a researcher12. We did not run a similar evaluation for the second stage used for flags from the completion-only classifier, and we also regularly update the exact filters used in the second stage without evaluating its effect on recall. We have analyzed a number of the thinking traces generated by our monitors and believe they are reasonably faithful and do not fail to disclose information they notice. We also found that our overall pipeline surfaced several of the most important dangerous actions that were taken during Mythos Preview’s deployment, like the ones described in Section 4.1.1 of the Mythos Preview System Card. The pipeline additionally surfaced several instances of dishonesty that had not been otherwise detected. Two incidents in which Mythos Preview (inadvertently) mass-deleted cluster jobs were flagged at the exchange level but not surfaced through the pipeline, which was likely due to the second stage of the pipeline’s emphasis on high risk pathways (even if they still represent some clear violation of user intent which we would like it to surface). We did not run end-to-end red-teaming on transcripts that were generated adversarially. 12 Some content redacted here for intellectual property protection. 5.5.1.3 Offline monitoring during training and evaluations The automated offline monitoring described above only covers a minority of sandboxed agentic usage. In particular, it does not cover reinforcement learning and most evaluations.
